title: Bristol F2B, pilot (IL-2 Great Battles)

sources.title: JoyPro cockpit catalog (from the IL-2 and real aircraft manuals)

intro: The Bristol F2B is a British two-seat biplane of the First World War. The pilot sits in front and has a Vickers gun and a plain instrument board. The observer sits behind and works the Lewis guns on a ring. This guide lists the pilot's seat and the observer's fittings.

areas.name: Gunsight
areas.text: This is the top of the instrument panel where the gunsight sits.

panels.name: Sight and gun
panels.text: This is the machine gun and the sight at the front of the cockpit.
panels.context: The pilot aims with the sight, and clears a stoppage by working the cocking handle.

controls.name: Aldis sight
controls.text: This is a small telescope used as a gunsight. It shows the target magnified with a mark in the picture and sits between or above the guns.
controls.context: The pilot looks through it to aim.

controls.name: Ring and bead sight
controls.text: This is a plain metal ring with a small bead in front of it, the old way of aiming. The pilot looks through the ring and puts the bead on the target.
controls.context: It is the backup aiming device when the main sight is broken, and on the oldest planes the way of aiming at all.

controls.name: Vickers cocking handle
controls.text: This is the handle that loads the machine gun, called cocking. If a round jams, the pilot works it to clear the stoppage.
controls.context: The pilot cocks the gun on the ground before take-off. In the air it clears a stoppage and the gun fires again.

areas.name: Instrument panel
areas.text: This is the panel in front of the pilot with the flight and engine gauges and the main switches.

panels.name: Instrument board
panels.text: This is the instrument board, a simple board with very few gauges and the switches for the engine. First World War planes have few instruments.
panels.context: The pilot flies mostly by eye and sound. The board only tells the basic things about the engine and the height.

controls.name: Rev counter
controls.text: This gauge shows how fast the engine turns, in turns per minute (RPM). The needle moves up as the engine speeds up.
controls.context: The pilot watches it when starting the engine and when setting power. On planes with a propeller lever, the lever sets this speed.

controls.name: Airspeed indicator
controls.text: This gauge shows how fast the plane moves through the air. The needle turns further round the dial as the plane gets faster.
controls.context: The pilot watches it all the time. Too slow and the wings stop lifting the plane, too fast and the plane can be damaged. It shows speed through the air, not speed over the ground.

controls.name: Altimeter
controls.text: This is the height gauge. Its needles show how high the plane is above the sea.
controls.context: The pilot checks it to stay clear of the ground and to hold the right height for a climb, a patrol or an attack. It reads the height from the air pressure outside.

controls.name: Magneto switches
controls.text: This is the ignition switch. It turns on the magnetos, the two small generators that make the sparks in the engine. Two are fitted for safety. The positions choose none, one or both.
controls.context: The pilot checks each magneto on its own before take-off and then runs on both. Without a magneto switched on the engine will not run.

positions.name: ON
positions.text: This position switches the equipment on.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: This position switches the equipment off.

controls.name: Radiator thermometer
controls.text: This gauge shows the temperature of the liquid that cools the engine. The liquid flows through the engine and then through a radiator that gives the heat to the air.
controls.context: If the needle goes too high, the pilot opens the radiator flaps or shutters so that more cooling air flows through. Too hot an engine can seize up.

controls.name: Oil pressure gauge
controls.text: This gauge shows the pressure of the engine oil. The oil lubricates the moving parts inside the engine, and the pump needs to push it round with enough pressure.
controls.context: The pilot checks it right after the engine starts. If the pressure is too low or falls during flight, the engine could be damaged.

controls.name: Air pressure gauge
controls.text: This gauge shows the air pressure in the fuel tank system. Air pressure pushes the fuel to the engine.
controls.context: The pilot builds the pressure with the hand pump and watches the gauge to keep it in the right range.

controls.name: Petrol tank selector
controls.text: This control chooses which fuel tank feeds the engine. The pilot turns it to a tank. Some planes have a pressure tank and a gravity tank.
controls.context: The pilot changes tanks when one runs low. The gravity tank is a backup that feeds the engine by gravity without a pump.

controls.name: Clock
controls.text: This is the clock. It shows the time of day, like a wall clock.
controls.context: The pilot uses it for timing, for example how long a certain course has been flown or when to be at a place. On long flights it helps to work out how much fuel is left.

controls.name: Compass
controls.text: This is the compass. A magnetised needle or card floats in a liquid and always points to north, so the pilot can read which way the plane is heading.
controls.context: It is the basic way to find the direction, and it works without any electricity. It swings about in turns, so the pilot reads it in straight flight.

areas.name: Left side wall
areas.text: This is the left wall of the cockpit. It holds the engine and everyday controls within reach of the left hand.

panels.name: Engine levers
panels.text: These are the engine levers on the left side of the cockpit. They set the power and the fuel flow of the engine, and the trim.
panels.context: The pilot's left hand rests on them in flight.

controls.name: Throttle
controls.text: This lever sets how much power the engine makes. Pushing it forward gives more power and the plane goes faster, pulling it back gives less.
controls.context: The pilot uses it all the time, at full power for take-off and a fight and at less power for cruising. It works like the gas pedal of a car.

controls.name: Altitude mixture lever
controls.text: This lever makes the mixture of fuel and air leaner as the plane climbs. Higher up the air is thinner, so less fuel is needed.
controls.context: The pilot adjusts it during a climb. Too rich a mixture at height makes the engine run roughly and waste fuel.

controls.name: Tailplane incidence wheel
controls.text: This handwheel tilts the tailplane, the small horizontal wing at the back, to trim the plane. It sets the nose a bit up or down so that the plane flies straight without holding the stick.
controls.context: The pilot turns it after take-off and when the speed changes, until the stick feels light.

controls.name: Radiator shutter lever
controls.text: This control opens or closes the flaps or shutters of the radiator, the part that cools the engine liquid. Open flaps let in more cooling air and also add air drag.
controls.context: The pilot opens them when the engine gets hot, for example on the ground or in a slow climb, and closes them in fast flight to reduce drag. The temperature gauge shows the need.

areas.name: Observer's seat
areas.text: This is the seat behind the pilot where the observer sits and works the Lewis guns.

panels.name: Observer's cockpit
panels.text: This is the observer's cockpit behind the pilot, with the Lewis guns on a ring. The observer is the crew member who shoots to the rear.
panels.context: The pilot flies the plane so that the observer's guns cover the rear. In this guide the observer's items are listed for completeness.

controls.name: Scarff ring mounting
controls.text: This is a big ring around the observer's seat on which the Lewis guns turn. The observer swings the guns round on it to aim.
controls.context: It lets the observer fire to the sides and to the rear, where the pilot's own guns cannot reach.

controls.name: Lewis guns
controls.text: These are the Lewis machine guns of the observer, the crew member who sits behind the pilot. They can be single or a pair on a ring.
controls.context: The pilot flies the plane so that the observer's guns can cover the rear. The observer, not the pilot, fires them.

controls.name: Ammunition drum stowage
controls.text: This is the rack where spare ammunition drums for the Lewis guns are stored.
controls.context: The observer takes a full drum from the rack when the drum on the gun runs empty.

areas.name: Stick and throttle
areas.text: This is what the pilot holds in the hands: the stick or wheel with its buttons, and the throttle and engine levers with their controls.

panels.name: Control stick

controls.name: Control stick
controls.text: This is the control stick, the plane's main flight control. Pulling it back lifts the nose, pushing it forward lowers the nose, and moving it sideways rolls the plane.
controls.context: The pilot holds it with the right hand all the time, and the weapon buttons are on its grip. In the game it is mapped to the pitch and roll axes of the joystick.

controls.name: Vickers trigger
controls.text: This is the trigger for the plane's guns. Pressing it fires the guns, and releasing it stops them.
controls.context: The pilot fires in short bursts when the enemy fills the gunsight. The firing mode and the weapons depend on the plane and on the switches that arm the guns.

panels.text: This is the control stick (or column) that the pilot holds with the right hand. Its grip carries the trigger, the firing button and other small controls.
panels.context: The pilot flies the plane with it all the time and fires the weapons with the buttons on its grip. In JoyPro each control of this panel can be given a button or axis on the joystick.

panels.name: Throttle and engine levers

controls.name: Throttle
controls.text: This is the throttle lever. Pushing it forward gives the engine more power, and pulling it back gives less. It works like the gas pedal of a car.
controls.context: The pilot uses it all the time. In the game it is mapped to the throttle axis of the joystick.

controls.name: Altitude mixture lever
controls.text: This is the altitude mixture lever, which makes the mixture of fuel and air leaner when the plane climbs.
controls.context: The thinner air higher up needs less fuel. The pilot moves the lever back during a climb and forward again on the way down.

controls.name: Radiator shutter control
controls.text: This lever opens and closes the radiator flaps or shutters by hand. The radiator cools the engine's coolant liquid, and open flaps let in more cooling air.
controls.context: The pilot opens it when the engine gets hot and closes it in fast flight to reduce air drag.

controls.name: Tailplane incidence wheel
controls.text: This handwheel tilts the tailplane, the small horizontal wing at the back, to trim the plane. It sets the nose a bit up or down so that the plane flies straight without holding the stick. The catalog lists it as 'Tailplane incidence wheel' in the Throttle and engine levers panel.
controls.context: The pilot turns it after take-off and when the speed changes, until the stick feels light. This entry is the one called 'Tailplane incidence wheel'.

panels.text: These are the engine and trim controls that the pilot's left hand works: the throttle, the propeller and mixture levers, the cooling control and the trim controls.
panels.context: They sit on the left side of the cockpit or on a pedestal. In JoyPro each control of this panel can be given a button or axis on the joystick or the throttle.
